phonemes.desc: Syllable with lateral approximant [l], diphthong [aʊ̯] (like 'ow' in 'cow'), and Tone 3 (falling-rising, ˨˩). The character 老 means 'old'.
Syllable with unaspirated alveolo-palatal affricate [ts], high front vowel [i], and Tone 3 (falling-rising). The character 子 is an honorific 'master' or 'venerable'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'LAOW-dzuh' — 'lao' like 'loud' without the final 'd', with a dipping tone (down then up); 'zi' like 'dzuh' with the same dipping tone.

pronunciation.note: Lǎozǐ is Tier 1: the tone marks on both syllables preserve the Mandarin citation tones — diacritics the ASCII form loses. The name means 'Old Master,' an honorific rather than a personal name. Whether Lǎozǐ was a historical figure, a composite, or a symbolic founder remains debated among scholars.

domains.title: The Old Master
domains.subtitle: Dao, Wuwei, and the Art of Ruling by Not Ruling
domains.lead: Lǎozǐ is the legendary author of the Dàodé Jīng, the founding text of Daoism and one of the most translated books on earth. His name means simply 'Old Master,' and the figure behind it is as elusive as the philosophy he teaches. Whether archivist, composite, or symbol, he gave Chinese thought its most radical sentence: the way that can be told is not the eternal way.

cards.name: The Dao
cards.desc: The unnamable source of all things; empty yet inexhaustible, it gives birth to heaven and earth.

cards.name: Wuwei
cards.desc: Acting without forced interference, like water that wears down stone by yielding.

cards.name: Uncarved Block
cards.desc: The pǔ, primal simplicity before society carves people into roles, names, and desires.

cards.name: Sage Ruler
cards.desc: The ideal leader governs by emptying hearts and filling bellies, keeping people simple and content.

mythology.lead: Lǎozǐ's mythology is inseparable from the biography invented for him by later tradition and from the enigmatic poems of the Dàodé Jīng. The sage is less a character in narrative than the voice of a teaching, but stories gathered around him to give that teaching a body.

myths.title: The Departure at Hán Gǔ Guān
myths.text: Sīmǎ Qiān's Shǐjì (chapter 63) records the most influential biography of Lǎozǐ, and it is a story about a book. Weary of the Zhou court's decay, the old archivist mounted a water buffalo and rode west toward the frontier. At Hán Gǔ Guān, the pass keeper Yīn Xī — who had divined that a sage would pass and had watched the sky for a purple vapor — recognized him and would not let him through without leaving a record. Lǎozǐ sat and wrote five thousand characters in eighty-one short chapters, the Dàodé Jīng, 'Classic of the Way and its Power,' then passed beyond the pass and was never reliably seen again. The story turns the text into a deposit: wisdom compelled to leave one artifact at the edge of the known world before disappearing into the wilderness it describes. Later tradition made the crossing cosmic — the sage leaving history for the realm where the Dào has no name — and the water buffalo became his fixed attribute in a thousand paintings.

myths.title: The Nameless Origin
myths.text: The opening of the Dàodé Jīng is not a narrative myth but a cosmogony, and it dissolves the genre as it speaks: 'The Dào that can be told is not the eternal Dào; the name that can be named is not the eternal name. The nameless is the beginning of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things' (ch. 1). Chapter 42 sketches the generation in three lines — 'The Dào gives birth to One; One gives birth to Two; Two gives birth to Three; Three gives birth to the ten thousand things' — and immediately grounds that cosmos in paired opposites, yīn and yáng, 'harmonized by the blending of breaths.' Chapter 25 names the source itself: 'There is something formed from chaos, born before heaven and earth... I do not know its name, so I style it Dào.' Chapter 40 gives the whole process its motion: 'Reversal is the movement of the Dào.' The myth's point is anti-mythic: any story of the world's origin is already one of the ten thousand things, and the source keeps its silence.

myths.title: The Deification of Lǎozǐ
myths.text: By the Han dynasty, Lǎozǐ had been transformed from philosopher to god. The Tàipíng Jīng and the emerging Daoist canon identified him as the embodiment of the Dào itself, an eternal being who descends in successive bodies to reveal saving teachings whenever the world decays — the Dào become substance, substance become Lǎozǐ, as the later formula has it. The Táng imperial house, surnamed Lǐ, claimed descent from him; Emperor Gāozōng honored him in 666 CE as Tàishàng Xuányuán Huángdì, 'Supreme Emperor of the Mysterious Origin,' and temples received state support. In organized Daoism he became Tàishàng Lǎojūn, 'the Most High Lord Lao,' enthroned among the highest deities of the pantheon — the uncarved archivist made into the fixed center of a religion's heaven. The apotheosis completed the journey in one direction: the man who wrote that 'the sage has no fixed heart-mind' became a celestial bureaucracy's most fixed star.

myths.title: The Dragon and the Teacher of Rites
myths.text: The Shǐjì sets Lǎozǐ's one recorded meeting against the greatest name in Chinese education. Confucius, says Sīmǎ Qiān, came to the capital to consult the archivist about the rites of antiquity — and Lǎozǐ received the question with open disdain: 'The men about whom you talk have mouldered, their bones are dust; only their words remain. Remove your pride and your many desires, your studied manner and your over-fond heart — these profit you nothing. That is all I have to say to you' (Shiji 63). Confucius withdrew and told his disciples: 'I know how birds fly, how fishes swim, how beasts run... but of the dragon I can say nothing — today I have seen Lǎozǐ, and he is like the dragon' (Shiji 63; Zhuāngzǐ 13 and 21 tell the meeting with variations). The scene gave Chinese philosophy its two poles in a single encounter: the teacher of ritual standing silent before the teacher of the wordless Way — and admitting that he had met something his categories could not hold.

lore.syncretism: Lǎozǐ and his text shaped not only Daoism but Chinese Buddhism, Confucianism, aesthetics, medicine, and statecraft. Early Chinese Buddhists used Daoist terms to translate Indian concepts, a process that permanently colored East Asian Buddhism. Neo-Confucian thinkers like Zhōu Dūnyí and Zhū Xī absorbed Daoist cosmology even while criticizing its quietism. In the modern West, Lǎozǐ became an icon of ecological thinking, anarchism, and mystical spirituality, though these readings often detach him from his political and ritual contexts. The Dàodé Jīng has been translated into more languages than any other Chinese text, making Lǎozǐ a global symbol of wisdom beyond words.
lore.culturalLegacy: Lǎozǐ's influence is woven into the texture of East Asian civilization. The Dàodé Jīng is studied, memorized, and quoted from childhood to old age; its aphorisms inform Chinese calligraphy, painting, martial arts, medicine, and governance. Daoist temples honor him as a deity, while scholars continue to debate the date, authorship, and meaning of his book. In the global marketplace of ideas, Lǎozǐ represents an alternative to Western activism and dualism: the sage who wins by yielding, who acts by not acting, and who finds power in emptiness. The Unicode restoration Lǎozǐ preserves the Mandarin tones that distinguish his name from the ordinary words for 'old' and 'master.'
lore.extendedMeditation:
Lǎozǐ is the teacher of the vanishing point. His Dao is not a doctrine to grasp but a way to fall into, like water finding the lowest place. Every definition fails because definition itself is the act of carving what was whole.

To read him is to be invited to do less, want less, and defend less. In a culture addicted to effort, Lǎozǐ proposes that the highest action resembles inaction, that the softest thing overcomes the hardest, and that the sage's power lies in being empty enough to receive the whole world.

lore.archaeology: The earliest manuscripts of the Dàodé Jīng were discovered at Mawangdui (c. 168 BCE) and Guodian (c. 300 BCE), predating the received text and showing the fluidity of the tradition. These silk and bamboo manuscripts are among the most important archaeological finds for early Chinese thought. Images of Lǎozǐ appear in Han tomb art and in later Daoist iconography as an aged sage riding an ox. Major Daoist temples and palace complexes preserve steles with imperial prefaces to the Dàodé Jīng, and the supposed site of Hán Gǔ Guān remains a place of pilgrimage.
